Episode Description:

Two coral fragments fell over in a Stanford lab tank and happened to touch, and within days the bleached one started absorbing healthy algae directly through the contact point with its neighbor. The researchers hadn’t designed that experiment, which is part of what makes the discovery so striking: a potential recovery mechanism for bleached coral hiding in plain sight, requiring nothing more than the right genetic match and direct physical contact.

Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including a brain therapy reporting 68 percent remission for PTSD when decades of medication have only reached 11, a wildlife sanctuary in Austin that runs on Twitch donations and reaches the conservation audience that broadcast nature documentaries never could, and the solar panels now legal for California renters that require no contractor, no roof, and no tens of thousands of dollars upfront.

Karissa:

Yeah.

Arielle:

And this is based in Sardinia, uh, which is in Italy. And there, the communal meal carries a lot of cultural weight. Yeah. I mean, it carries weight everywhere because eating is such a social human practice. But in Italy especially, if the-

Karissa:

Yeah …

Arielle:

dinner table is losing to screens over there, then that’s a, a real signal. The next solution is titled “California legalizes balcony solar for renters and beyond”. So there’s no contractor, no roof, no tens of thousands of dollars upfront for Californians who live in apartments. California is the 10th state to pass this kind of law.

It’s the biggest electricity market in the country, so when California moves, then manufacturers basically have to follow. The goal advocates keep describing is plug-in solar on a shelf at a hardware store like any other appliance, and that’s finally a realistic near-term thing.

First green star discovered

The next solution is a pretty fun one.

It’s titled “Astronomers discovered first green star ever, and it’s powered by a dead planet’s chemistry”. A star that ate its planets and turned green.

It’s like a sci-fi. I was just- Yeah … fascinated by this whole solution. Uh, but yeah, I just found the whole thing quite interesting. I just think it’s really cool to think about all of this unexpected, completely surprising stuff happening in this universe.

It’s 478,000 hectares of protected habitat, which is roughly 1.2 million acres, and the thing that finally made it financially viable was carbon credits. The part about carbon credits is what makes the economics work. The government registered over 117,000 hectares of the park state forests with the Federal Clean Energy Regulator.

By ending native forest logging there, they can now sell carbon credits from the land. Protected forest generates more revenue than logged timber, it turns out, and that’s the financial argument that helped get this through. The article goes into the human cost. It didn’t wanna glaze over that detail. The forestry corporation already cut 30-plus jobs in Coffs Harbour before the park was even finalized, and then there’s also timber suppliers and trucking companies, engineering firms, all of these places of employment that have to let a lot of people go.

So the government- Yeah … is committed to moving displaced workers into national parks roles, but that transition is still underway, and I’m sure it will go through some growing pains. Ashley Love, the conservationist who started this campaign after locals told him koalas weren’t as common as they used to be, called the result, “Quite fragmented with connectivity gaps still to close.”

Karissa:

Arielle:

Mm-hmm. It’s a win for the koalas, and a win for Australia’s broader biodiversity as a whole.

Coral healing through touch

Arielle:

The last solution that I’m going to share with everyone before I hand over the reins to Karissa is “Stanford scientists discovered bleached coral can heal through touch”. Two coral fragments accidentally fell over and touched each other in a Stanford lab tank.

Within days, the fragment that was bleached started recovering, absorbing healthy algae directly through the point of contact with the healthy coral fragment. The researchers were blown away because this was not supposed to happen. It was not really their experiment at all. What makes it scientifically interesting is how specific the conditions have to be for this to happen.

It only works with direct physical contact and only between genetically identical corals. If you separate them by a few millimeters, then nothing will happen. If you introduce a different genetic background, then they reject each other, much like a mismatched organ transplant. Genetic twins in contact create what the team calls a tissue bridge, which is a nutrient highway between them The IUCN announced that about 96% of the world’s shallow water reef systems are critically endangered and could disappear by 2075.

Coral reefs support between a quarter and a third of all marine species, so this discovery is a glimmer of hope in a very dark picture.

Okay, so this is one of our local Change

lived in Big Bear Lake, I think captured the hearts of many. So once again, congrats to Maya, and check out the article for more details.

Solar kits for disaster relief

Karissa:

The next solution is “Solar kits are changing what disaster relief looks like”. Every morning in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo and tarpaulin shelter and puts out a solar panel.

He’s done it for six years since his family fled the Rohingya crackdown in Myanmar. That one panel is how his whole family charges phones, cooks with light, and keeps fans running through the heat. But I don’t really think about it in this context where it could be so, so useful for disaster relief or- Yeah

for places that don’t have access to a reliable grid. Uh, so I think it’s really encouraging that this technology is reaching all corners of the world for all types of contexts and situations.

Household uses for toothpaste

Karissa:

The next story is a lifestyle solution, and it’s “Eight surprising household uses for toothpaste from a pro cleaner”.

So there’s probably a tube of toothpaste in your bathroom right now, and if it’s only going on your teeth, you’re leaving a surprisingly useful cleaning tool just sitting in the drawer. A professional cleaner shared the eight household jobs she regularly uses it for, and some of them are actually not that obvious.

Plain, white, non-gel toothpaste has mild abrasive particles that work like an ultra-fine sandpaper, and that’s why it can buff out light scratches on glass, phone screens, and wood surfaces, and polish metal fixtures, so lots of different uses. Gel toothpaste doesn’t have those particles, so it doesn’t work the same way, and that’s just something to keep in mind when you reach for that toothpaste.

One use I was surprised to read is using toothpaste for a fogged car headlight, and it’s one that a lot of people haven’t heard, and it’s really simple. You just rub toothpaste over the lens in small circles for about a minute or two, rinse, dry, and repeat if needed. So no specialty product is required to clear up those fogged headlights.

There’s just kind of this huge appetite right now, especially with the economy and the whole idea of sustainability as well, to, you know, use things you already own and get creative with them. It’s practical, it’s low cost, and it’s also satisfying as well.

Brain therapy for PTSD

Karissa:

Moving on to the next solution, “Personalized brain therapy hits 68% remission for PTSD”.

The best FDA-approved medications for PTSD have a remission rate of about 11%. But a newly FDA-cleared brain therapy just reported a 68% remission, and that’s not a typo. That is a big difference. It’s the first non-drug treatment specifically cleared for PTSD since the diagnosis was formally recognized in 1980.

How this therapy works is that you get an EEG that maps your specific brain electrical activity, and an AI algorithm builds a personalized stimulation plan from that data. Then a coil placed against your scalp delivers targeted magnetic pulses, and you do this for five sessions a week for five to six weeks.

The lead researcher described standard brain stimulation as covering the leak with a tarp, and this treatment tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. This is important for many different populations because about 6% of Americans will experience PTSD in their lifetime with higher rates among women and veterans.

Approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day in the US. The two SSRIs approved for PTSD have been the only FDA-approved options since 1980, and 11% remission means the vast majority haven’t gotten there on medications alone. So this is a really great breakthrough, and of course, accessibility is going to be the next hurdle.

Um, you know, teams are actively trying to work on getting this covered by insurance, and FDA clearance is not the same as accessibility, so this gap is the next fight

Volunteering this Thanksgiving

Karissa:

The final solution I have to share is “The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving, 17 options for every schedule”. Every year around Thanksgiving, a lot of people have the same thought, “This is the year I actually do something.”

And then they show up at a food bank and find out every other person in town had the same idea. There’s actually a smarter way to do this, and several options that don’t even require leaving your couch at all. So I think the most important point out of this article, even though it gives tips to volunteer and help around, is that holiday demand often creates more volunteers than organizations can actually use on Thanksgiving Day itself.

And a lot of that is directed at food banks. So if you want your time to count, definitely call ahead and see if you’re needed. And if you get redirected because a location is at capacity, ask when they need people the most. The answer is almost always in February, when the holiday energy has faded out, but the need hasn’t.

And I think that’s just a really good point. These organizations need your help year-round, and that’s important to keep in mind. So this list covers every kind of situation, whether it’s Feeding America, Meals on Wheels, and Operation Turkey, and about the tightly organized shifts they have. But it also covers options that are remote, like writing letters to deployed service members through Support Our Troops, and animal shelters for people who are better with dogs than crowds.

So lots of ways to volunteer this giving, thankful, grateful season. So yeah, I think it’s just a great reminder, and hard to believe that Thanksgiving is already around the corner.

Arielle:

Yeah, I totally agree. I, I didn’t really think too much about the oversaturation in the volunteering space for the holiday season.

It does make sense, though. So, you know, I, I think if you’re interested in volunteering and just haven’t gotten around to it yet, then maybe the holiday season is a great place to start. But then it could be your gateway into doing it-

Karissa:

Yeah …

Arielle:

more regularly as well.

Outro & quote

Karissa:

Well, that’s all of the positive news we had to share this week on The Optimist Daily.

But before we go, we’ll leave you off with a quote. ”

Arielle:

Having a good time together is the essence of lovingness and the best means of increasing it.” That’s from Benjamin Spock, and I think that’s a great quote to go with quite a few of our stories today.

Karissa:

Yeah, exactly. That’s why I wanted to include it in today’s, uh, roundup.

Arielle:

We will be back next week with more solutions. In the meantime, Karissa and I wish all of you Optimists and Emissaries a wonderful weekend.

Karissa:

Yeah. Bye, everyone.

Bye.

articles.title: Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows, and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The surprising discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect.
articles.content:
Picture the wilderness of central Europe 100,000 years ago, or even a million years ago. You might imagine an endless expanse of towering trees, with thick canopies blocking sunlight from reaching the ground. But according to a major new study, that familiar image of Europe's ancient forests is probably misleading.

Instead, much of the continent was a vibrant landscape of scattered trees, open woodlands, grassy clearings, and colorful wildflower meadows. Birds and butterflies flourished in these sunlit habitats, while enormous grazing animals helped prevent trees and shrubs from taking over.

Researchers led by Aarhus University have found that this mixture of habitats dominated Europe's landscapes for more than 20 million years. Far from being the continent's original natural condition, the dense, dark forests common in many parts of Europe today appear to be a relatively recent development in its ecological history.

Published in Biological Conservation, the findings challenge a longstanding assumption about what Europe's wilderness looked like before widespread human intervention. They also raise important questions about modern reforestation programs, which often prioritize planting dense forests to combat climate change and protect biodiversity.

"The study shows that current reforestation practices are on the wrong track - both here in Denmark, where subsidies are only granted for planting dense forests, and elsewhere in Europe. This will not only be harmful for biodiversity; it will be in direct contradiction to the type of ecosystems that Europe's species have evolved in over millions of years," says Professor Jens-Christian Svenning from the Center for Ecological Dynamics in a Novel Biosphere (ECONOVO), Department of Biology at Aarhus University, senior author of the study.

Challenging the Myth of Europe's Ancient Forests

For decades, conservation strategies have been influenced by the "closed-forest paradigm." This is the belief that dense forests with nearly continuous tree canopies were Europe's natural landscape before humans began clearing land for agriculture and settlements.

Under this view, restoring nature often means allowing trees to reclaim open areas or planting forests where they no longer exist.

The new research suggests that this approach may overlook a crucial part of Europe's ecological history. Rather than being uniformly covered by dense forests, the continent was characterized by changing combinations of grasslands, shrubs, and woodlands with different amounts of tree cover.

These landscapes supported a rich variety of species adapted to both wooded and open environments. Large plant-eating animals also played a major role in maintaining this diversity by grazing, browsing, and disturbing vegetation.

What 23 Million Years of Evidence Reveals

To reconstruct Europe's ancient environments, the researchers examined an unusually extensive collection of evidence spanning millions of years.

Previous studies have generally concentrated on more recent periods. This investigation extended much further into the past, examining paleoecological records from the Miocene epoch (which began around 23 million years ago) through the pre-industrial era.

Paleoecology is the study of ancient ecosystems using clues preserved in fossils, sediments, and other natural records. Because no single type of evidence can provide a complete picture of the distant past, the team combined several independent methods.

These included fossilized pollen and larger plant remains, charcoal left by ancient wildfires, and chemical signatures preserved in the teeth and bones of plant-eating animals. The researchers also examined fossil insects and mammals, along with ancient environmental DNA recovered from sediments.

Environmental DNA consists of genetic material left behind by organisms in their surroundings. When preserved in ancient deposits, it can help scientists identify plants and animals that lived in an area long ago.

Together, these different sources of evidence allowed the researchers to reconstruct not only what types of vegetation existed, but also how ecosystems changed over time and how animals influenced their surroundings.

"Each type of proxy offers its own perspective, but together they let us see whether the landscapes were covered by dense forests, open grasslands, or a mix of the two. By combining these datasets across time - from the Miocene to the pre-industrial era - we could trace long-term changes in vegetation and the role of large herbivores with much greater confidence than earlier studies that used only one method," explains the study's lead author, ECONOVO PhD student Szymon Czyzewski of Aarhus University.

The evidence points to a consistent pattern. Across more than 20 million years, Europe's landscapes were typically a shifting mosaic of trees, open spaces, and flowering plants rather than continuous stretches of closed forest.

Importantly, these mixed landscapes were not limited to one particular climate. They existed under temperate conditions comparable to those in much of Europe today, as well as during warmer and colder periods.

Elephants, Rhinos, and Bison Shaped Europe's Wilderness

One of the most striking findings concerns the influence of large wild herbivores.

Ancient Europe was home to animals such as elephants, rhinoceroses, aurochs, and bison. By feeding on vegetation and disturbing the ground as they moved, these animals helped keep parts of the landscape open.

Their activities created opportunities for grasses, wildflowers, and other plants that might otherwise have struggled beneath dense tree cover.

This constant interaction between animals and vegetation helped sustain a diverse mixture of habitats, providing suitable conditions for many different species.

Modern Europe, however, is missing much of this ecological influence. Many of the large wild herbivores that once shaped its landscapes have disappeared, and traditional grazing practices have also declined.

"The ecosystems we see in Europe today lack the large wild herbivores that not only shaped landscapes but also sustained its biodiversity for millions of years. The most dramatic shift has largely taken place within the last hundred years, when traditional extensive grazing disappeared from large parts of the landscape," says Czyzewski.

This loss of grazing pressure has changed how vegetation develops across much of the continent, helping explain why present-day European ecosystems differ so dramatically from those of the distant past.

Europe's Ancient Woodlands Were Full of Wildflowers

The research also offers a different perspective on species commonly associated with farmland and other human-managed environments.

Birds such as larks and jackdaws, along with mammals such as the European hamster, are often regarded as characteristic of agricultural landscapes. Yet the researchers suggest that their evolutionary histories likely extend back to the open woodland environments that existed long before modern farming.

Even familiar wildflowers have connections to these ancient ecosystems.

Wild poppies, now frequently seen growing in agricultural fields, also thrived in areas where large grazing animals disturbed vegetation within ancient woodlands.

These findings challenge the sharp distinction between "forest" and "open habitats" that often guides conservation planning today.

In Europe's ecological past, trees, meadows, shrubs, and grazing animals were not necessarily separate parts of nature. They frequently existed together, forming interconnected habitats that supported a wide range of wildlife.

Why Planting More Trees May Not Always Help Nature

The findings arrive as European countries continue expanding forests to capture carbon dioxide, address climate change, and restore biodiversity.

Although forests can provide important environmental benefits, the researchers argue that planting large areas of uniformly dense woodland may not be the best approach when the goal is to restore Europe's native ecosystems.

Many European species evolved in landscapes containing a mixture of trees and open areas. Converting these habitats into continuous closed-canopy forests could therefore reduce the variety of environments available to wildlife.

The study suggests that restoration efforts should focus more strongly on maintaining diverse landscapes, including open grasslands, scattered woodland, and areas shaped by natural grazing.

"Instead, restoration efforts should place greater emphasis on creating and maintaining mosaics of woodland and open habitats - not least through the restoration of natural-living large herbivores," Svenning concludes.

The findings add to a growing body of research from the same scientific group suggesting that large animals played a far greater role in shaping Europe's ecosystems than previously recognized.

They also reinforce the idea that Europe's ancient landscapes were generally brighter, more open, and more varied than the dense primeval forests often depicted in popular imagination.

Rather than restoring nature by simply planting more trees, the researchers suggest that protecting biodiversity may require recreating the complex balance of woodlands, meadows, and grazing animals that shaped the continent for millions of years.

The familiar image of Europe as a vast, dark, unbroken forest may be deeply rooted in our understanding of nature, but millions of years of evidence are painting a very different picture.

articles.title: Glaciers around the world are endangered — but no two are alike
articles.content:
Part of my work as a geographer and glacier scientist involves traveling around the world. Literally. Several times a year, I join expeditions, traversing continents and oceans, sometimes half the planet, in mere days. I’ve visited glaciers in some startling places — like Uganda’s Stanley Glacier, where ice retreat influences human health and malaria outbreaks. Or Iceland’s Breiðamerkurjökull, where glacier change is exacerbating the ice-breaking pressures of global tourism. Or South Georgia’s Heaney Glacier, where ice retreat has provided expansive real estate for one of the largest King penguin colonies on Earth.

My job is to translate the landscape: how oceans move nutrients pole to pole; why one mountain might support snow but another does not; how glaciers shape societies.

I’ll own it’s a peculiar way to experience the world.

From 30,000 feet, borders fall away. Trees become forests become systems become a living planet. I see connections everywhere. But that view from 30,000 feet, while striking, can miss much of what’s unfolding below at the individual level — the people, the lives, the histories.

Glaciers, I think, suffer from this same problem of perspective. We tend to see them from a great distance, as a single global story.

They’re tallied together: Some 275,000 individual glaciers remain worldwide. They’re measured together: how quickly they are shrinking, how much they impact sea level change, how long before they are gone. How many of them already are.

But glaciers have never lived identical lives. My work has shown over and over that every glacier has a distinct life history, shaped by and shaping the communities, landscapes, and systems around it. As glaciers change, we aren’t witnessing a single global glacier story from 30,000 feet. We are witnessing hundreds of thousands of individual stories of transformation.

One of the most surprising is unfolding right in my own backyard.

In the Pacific Northwest, a young glacier is growing

An aerial view of Mount St. Helens in June 2024, with Mount Hood in the distance on the left. USGS

My most recent expedition took me to nine countries. But I started the trip in Portland, Oregon — just north of my home in Eugene — land of the exhilaratingly perfect medium roast coffee and the Cascade volcano chain I used to orient myself for most of my childhood. The first morning, I ran up to the hotel’s top floor to see if the weather was clear enough to peer 50 miles northeast toward Mount St. Helens, across the border in Washington state. From downtown, it is easy to distinguish her whaleback summit, notably slumped in comparison to the sharper profiles of Mount Hood and Mount Adams.

What isn’t visible from this distance is the secret Mount St. Helens is hiding within.

The volcano erupted in May of 1980, two years before I was born. I grew up hearing stories of how ash coated our family farm, how the afternoon sky turned murky, how one terrified horse kicked through her box stall door. What I didn’t learn until much, much later was that, prior to the eruption, Mount St. Helens supported 11 named glaciers and two small unnamed ones. The nine-hour Plinian eruption destroyed 70 percent of the mountain’s ice, including the Loowit and Leschi glaciers, while the summit and entire north flank collapsed, leaving behind a horseshoe-shaped crater roughly two miles wide.

If you’ve ever received a climbing permit from the U.S. Forest Service, hiked to the crater rim, and gazed into that windy bowl of pumice and dark basalts, I can almost guarantee the very last word on your mind is “nursery.” Trust me. I rocked my baby in a softly-lit Scandinavian-paletted room designed for every possible infant need. But Mount St. Helens, apparently a fan of free-range parenting, took another approach. And it worked. Inside that raw volcanic maw, a baby glacier is growing inside.

The eruption that destroyed most of Mount St. Helens’ glaciers also created the perfect conditions to grow a new one.

Winter after winter, snow fell on the volcano’s steep headwall, and then it avalanched, repeatedly, into the crater floor below. By September 1996, scientists observed that the 16-year-old body of snow and ice had begun to move, flow. This fact is existential — glaciers are defined as moving bodies of land ice that persist year after year. When glaciers stop moving, they are “dead” — it’s not just loss of volume that threatens their identity as glaciers. The Okjökull glacier in Iceland was declared dead in 2014 when it stopped flowing; in 2019, the nation held a funeral for it.

But here, the opposite has happened.

Welcome to the world, Crater Glacier.

A view of Crater Glacier in 2005. M Jackson

There is something equally wonderful and strange about being almost exactly the same age as a glacier. We’re both children of the 80s, who grew up under the same Cascade volcanoes. I became a glaciologist; she became a glacier.

And we’ve both had setbacks. Me: paying my bills, becoming a mother, and learning, repeatedly, that adulthood rarely follows the topography you planned.

Crater Glacier: Mount St. Helens, in 2004, erupted again. Magma began pushing up beneath her. A lava dome swelled through the crater floor and into the glacier itself — the first time scientists observed the emplacement of a lava dome through glacier ice.

It split her in two.

As the dome grew, the now separate arms of the glacier deformed, then thickened and sped up, flowing 1 to 2 feet (30 to 60 centimeters) per day. Within four years, those arms stretched all the way around the lava dome and rejoined. And the glacier kept going. Between 2009 and 2019, she gained some 13.8 million cubic meters of ice and advanced more than a thousand feet.

My colleagues have noted that her advance is slowing. Eventually, warming Pacific Northwest summers may overwhelm the unique climate zone inside Mount St. Helens’ crater. Or, the volcano might erupt again.

And that matters to the people living below.

Crater Glacier’s body wraps around an active vent and lava dome. A future eruption could melt ice, mix with ash, pumice, and rock and become a lahar, a fast-moving slurry of water, mud, trees, and whatever else it picks up as it races downslope. Lahars from the 1980 eruption destroyed homes, bridges, and roads. Growing up, I remember how we were taught drills for lahars alongside earthquakes and fires.

It isn’t lost on me how radically the landscape I grew up with has changed, or how much more it will change in the years to come. But, as I follow Crater Glacier’s development, I’m reminded that it isn’t all bad. This one glacier, among hundreds of thousands, is writing a story I could never have imagined.

In Azerbaijan, forgotten glaciers become much-needed water

I arrive in Baku, Azerbaijan, in July. It is sweltering.

This country has glaciers, but I won’t see them on this trip. The last time I saw ice in the Caucasus, I was on a Fulbright in Turkey, living on the Black Sea and exploring these mountains from the west. The ice I saw then would be unrecognizable today.

Between 2000 and 2020, Azerbaijan lost 77 percent of the country’s total glacier area.

To me, that’s baffling to think about: 77 percent. Over 20 years. Half my life.

And yet, almost no one I meet in Azerbaijan seems particularly interested in talking about glaciers. I risk distracting my driver, Kamran, a delightful 20-something local man who weaves through Baku’s insane, seven-lanes-of-madness traffic like it’s nothing. The Caspian Sea twinkles peacefully to our left, oil derricks lazily chugging. To our right, the city’s iconic blue-gleaming high-rises overlap with mosques and war memorials.

A mud volcano at Gobustan State Historical and Cultural Reserve in Azerbaijan. M Jackson

“We don’t bother with them,” Kamran tells me, speaking of the glaciers. He pivots quickly to Gobustan, a district south of Baku that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Had I seen the mud volcanoes? “Tourists come all the time now to see the methane volcanoes.”

I keep encountering this indifference. My colleague, Suleyman, also doesn’t want to talk about glaciers and spends the bulk of our coffee telling me about the pending F1 race in Baku. He doesn’t even bother glancing at the map I’ve brought. Azerbaijan’s glaciers are remote, tiny, and high in the Eastern Caucasus. By 2025, 14 fragmented glaciers remain, covering together about 124 acres — roughly one-tenth of the ice that covered these mountains in the 1890s.

But glaciers here, like glaciers everywhere, are critical components of regional water cycles. Glaciers hold water — for years, decades, centuries. They are reservoirs that do not need to be constructed. And in Azerbaijan, water and water storage matter. Agriculture relies on a complex system of reservoirs, canals, and irrigation. Groundwater withdrawals have increased some fourfold since 2000, largely fueled by farms growing wheat, fruit, and vegetables.

In 2025, researchers climbed Azerbaijan’s Tufandag Glacier and reported retreat, accelerated melting, and expanding crevasses. Below it, the Mahmuddara River had increased water levels and discharge rates.

This is how a glacier can disappear in plain sight: by transforming into liquid. As a glacier melts, it releases more water downstream. And for that reason, the current precipitous decline of Azerbaijan’s glaciers is almost a boon. Glacier becomes meltwater, river, irrigation, drinking water, wheat, lettuce, peaches. Farmers rejoice.

But, eventually, too much ice dissolves and the runoff peaks, then decreases. In glaciology, we call this “peak water,” when a disappearing glacier gives us the most water it ever will. The cycle of savings and withdrawals that has defined this landscape for centuries will ultimately end like this, when the bank is forced to close.

Has Tufandag Glacier, or any of Azerbaijan’s 13 other glaciers, crossed that threshold? I don’t know. The increased flow of the Mahmuddara is only one measurement, from one glacier, that cannot fully answer that question.

But I can think back to the ice I saw in these same mountains years ago, then look at the Caucasus today, and I understand that it has transformed. Water that was ice, storage, cold is now warm liquid moving downstream.

Azerbaijan’s remaining glaciers may not survive this century. People in the coming years are going to have to do what glaciers once did — come up with more ways to store more water. Catch it when it arrives and hold it until it’s needed.

I keep thinking about the apparent indifference many Azerbaijanis show towards glaciers. Maybe Kamran’s response is more revealing than I initially thought.

Perhaps the first step of a glacier disappearing from a landscape is it disappearing from conversation.

In Japan, newly discovered glaciers are already fading

A view out the window of a plane of Kuranosuke Glacier in Japan.

M Jackson

If you ever get a chance, wander through the Tateyama Museum in Toyama Prefecture, Japan. The exquisite open-air museum explores the nearby Mount Tateyama as both landscape and sacred place: a perennially snow-covered mountain, a dwelling place of spirits and the dead, a realm containing hell and heaven.

There is a poem there by the eighth-century poet Ōtomo no Yakamochi about Tateyama’s summer snow and its association with the divine. It stops me. Some 1,300 years ago, people were already writing — marveling — about the snow that refused to disappear.

Japan’s Sea-of-Japan side is one of the snowiest places on Earth, a skier’s powder paradise. And yet, for years, my colleagues and I thought no glaciers existed east of Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. The landscape was too warm, the mountains too low, to support glaciers under today’s conditions.

For glaciers — moving bodies of land ice that persist year after year — the base variables are critical: snow, time, and temperature. But those variables do interact with intensely local conditions such as wind, topography, shade — even human activity. It matters where snow falls, where it blows, and where a landscape and people allow it to accumulate.

Japan is technically not cold enough long enough to support glaciers. But it is extraordinarily snowy.

When I flew over Tateyama in June, most of the three-peaked massif was gray — alpine bare, with significant snow melt. But I did see a few Dalmatian-like white pockets in shaded nooks and north-facing crannies. If I hadn’t known better, I would have just labeled them as snow patches. Remember: Definitionally, a glacier must flow under its own weight. More movement is a sign of a healthy glacier.

Snow patches, regardless of how long they’ve existed or if they contain ice, do not move.

Everyone in the bustling world of cryospheric research knew Japan had snow patches. More than 100 had been identified in the northern Japanese Alps alone.

In the 1970s, researchers began observing holes in Kuranosuke — one such snow patch, roughly 6 acres in area — that looked and behaved like glacial features called moulins. In 1979, a Japanese researcher investigated one of the moulins by using the time-honored glaciological technique of climbing directly into it. He discovered layers of ancient ice, an observation supported later by radiocarbon analysis of embedded wood and leaf debris that were dated to approximately 1,700 years old.

Old, yes. But old does not make a glacier. Movement does.

And so Kuranosuke remained, scientifically speaking, for decades and decades, a snow patch.

Sunrise at the Kuranosuke hiking hut in the Northern Japanese Alps in July 2025. Antoine Boureau / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images

But then, starting in 2009, researchers Kotaro Fukui and Hajime Iida of the Tateyama Caldera Sabo Museum used state-of-the-art geodetic measurements and ground-penetrating radar to take a closer look at several well-known perennial snow patches in the Japanese Alps. They showed that the Gozenzawa, Sannomado, and Komado snow patches were, in fact, flowing. They were glaciers.

Take that in. I have spent my entire life watching ice disappear faster than we can understand it. Yet here are glaciers we never knew existed. It makes me immediately wonder — what other ones might be out there, if only we had time, resources, and the will to look?

The researchers turned to Kuranosuke next. They found that the snow patch was flowing roughly 3 centimeters a year — the equivalent width of one of the LEGO bricks my son always leaves on our stairs. An almost absurdly small measurement, but 3 centimeters is still flow. Movement. This transformed Kuranosuke from a snow patch into a glacier.

Still, identities are never quite so fixed. Recently, Kukui, Iida, and Tomoyoshi Kosaka have argued that Kuranosuke is in the midst of another slow transformation. As Japan warms, its glaciers and snow patches are losing crucial ice mass. They say that Kuranosuke is declining. It exists now in a nebulous no-scientist’s-land between glacier and snow patch, blurring the very boundaries of glacierhood.

One could easily look at that as a poignant story of loss: This glacier is dying, and we’ve barely had a chance to really know her. But when I look at Kuranosuke, I see a story of persistence. For at least 1,700 years, some form of ice and snow has held here, through centuries of summers, through blurring with the divine, through recognition as perennial snow patch and then glacier.

And now, glacier-in-transformation.

I don’t think the disappearance of Kuranosuke will diminish local people’s reverence for Tateyama. If anything, as the mountain’s once-perennial snow and ice disappear, Ōtomo no Yakamochi’s poem may take on even greater meaning. For 1,300 years, these words and this snow have persisted. We may be the last generation to witness them together.

For all these glaciers, and countless others, their stories are neither simple nor predictable. These are not merely stories of inches lost. If anything, they prove that we are far from certain about what the future holds. Kuranosuke and her neighbors defied decades of settled science by asserting their existence as glaciers. Tufandag is bringing abundance to the river and farms below it — though for how much longer, we don’t know. And Crater Glacier is still growing, thriving as so many others dissolve. I find something profoundly moving in that.

And me? I’m still circling the planet, collecting glacier stories. Maybe, like Ōtomo no Yakamochi’s poem, we’ll need them someday.

To remember.

Comprendre ces différences aide à mieux prévoir comment les glaciers influencent l’eau et les communautés.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les scientifiques continueront de surveiller les glaciers pour voir comment ils changent avec le temps. Ils étudieront comment l’eau de fonte soutient les populations et comment les volcans ou la montée des températures affectent la croissance ou la perte des glaciers. Ces connaissances aideront les communautés à mieux planifier leurs besoins en eau et à se préparer aux catastrophes naturelles comme les inondations causées par la fonte des glaciers.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Les glaciers du monde entier changent de façons très différentes, révélant des histoires surprenantes qui nous aident à comprendre les liens complexes entre la glace, la nature et les humains.
articles.personality_title_es: Los glaciares cuentan historias únicas: crecimiento, derretimiento y sorpresas para los científicos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los glaciares suelen verse como un problema global único que se está reduciendo en todas partes debido al cambio climático. Pero los científicos que estudian los glaciares en el mundo han descubierto que cada glaciar tiene su propia historia. Estos cuerpos de hielo tienen vidas diferentes, influenciadas por su ubicación, clima y las personas cercanas.

**Qué pasó** – Un científico de glaciares viajó a varios países y compartió tres historias importantes. Cerca del monte St. Helens en Estados Unidos, un nuevo glaciar llamado Crater Glacier ha estado creciendo desde la erupción volcánica de 1980. En Azerbaiyán, los glaciares se están derritiendo rápido, pero el agua de deshielo está ayudando a los agricultores al proporcionar agua para los cultivos. En Japón, los investigadores descubrieron que algunos parches de nieve son en realidad glaciares porque se mueven lentamente, aunque Japón es más cálido que las zonas típicas de glaciares.

**Impacto** – Estos ejemplos muestran que los glaciares no se comportan todos igual. Algunos pueden crecer incluso después de una gran erupción volcánica, como Crater Glacier. Otros, como los de Azerbaiyán, proporcionan agua que la gente necesita, pero podrían desaparecer pronto. El descubrimiento de nuevos glaciares en Japón desafía lo que los científicos pensaban posible en lugares más cálidos. Entender estas diferencias ayuda a predecir mejor cómo los glaciares afectan el agua y las comunidades.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán observando los glaciares para ver cómo cambian con el tiempo. Estudiarán cómo el agua de deshielo apoya a las personas y cómo los volcanes o el aumento de temperaturas afectan el crecimiento o pérdida de glaciares. Este conocimiento ayudará a las comunidades a planear mejor sus necesidades de agua y prepararse para desastres naturales como las inundaciones causadas por el deshielo.

**Una frase clave** – Los glaciares en todo el mundo están cambiando de muchas maneras diferentes, revelando historias sorprendentes que nos ayudan a entender la relación compleja entre el hielo, la naturaleza y las personas.

articles.title: From a ship frozen into Arctic ice, a warning to world leaders: Trust the science
articles.summary: Drifting through the polar darkness, a team of scientists is documenting a rapidly changing Arctic. As sea ice retreats and oil tankers move in, a conversation with the UN chief reveals why the battle for climate science matters far beyond the North Pole.
articles.content:
Somewhere in the darkness of the Arctic Ocean, 12 people and a dog named Örkki are drifting right now across the frozen sea, with little say over where they are going.

Their home for the winter is Tara Polar Station, a 26-metre-long French research vessel that departed Norway in August with an unusual purpose: to become trapped in ice.

Locked into a floating sheet of sea ice above more than 2,500 metres of water, the station moves wherever the winds and currents carry it. There is no destination to steer towards, and in the middle of the polar night, no sunlight to mark the passing days.

The team is taking part in Tara Polaris I, the first of 10 planned expeditions in a 20-year international programme to study the transformation of the Arctic Ocean. What they are already witnessing has caught the attention of UN Secretary-General António Guterres.

What happens in the Arctic doesn't stay in the Arctic.

Ahead of the COP31 UN climate conference, the UN chief spoke this week by video link to the expedition’s chief scientist, Maxime Geoffroy, asking what message he should take to world leaders about an Arctic which is warming three to four times faster than the global average.

“I think that, unfortunately, the political leadership in this world is not yet entirely aware of how serious the situation is,” the UN chief said.

Mr. Geoffroy’s message was simple: “What happens in the Arctic doesn't stay in the Arctic.”

The changes unfolding beneath the expedition’s feet could have far-reaching consequences for the world’s oceans, climate and biodiversity, he warned.

© Sébastien Devrient

A disappearing world

The mission draws inspiration from Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen, who famously allowed his vessel to freeze into Arctic sea ice in 1893 and drift with the currents.

More than 130 years later, Mr. Geoffroy and his colleagues are following in his footsteps, with one striking difference: there is considerably less ice in their way.

The expedition spent three weeks navigating along Russia's northern coast before heading into the Arctic ice pack in search of a suitable floe (a large flat piece of floating ice) for its research station.

“We reached 82 degrees north just through leads,” Mr. Geoffroy said, referring to channels of open water between the floes.

When Nansen made his voyage, his vessel became trapped in ice hundreds of kilometres farther south. Now, open stretches of water allowed Mr. Geoffroy's team to travel much deeper before becoming icebound.

But the retreating ice is only part of the story.

© Sébastien Devrient

The planet’s ‘mirror’ is melting

The Secretary-General asked Mr. Geoffroy about one of his greatest fears for the future:

“One of the things that has scared me most was the perspective that in a number of years we might have no ice in the Arctic, during summer.”

Arctic sea ice plays a vital role in regulating the Earth’s temperature and keeping the planet cool.

“This large ice sheet on which we are drifting, when the sun comes back, acts as a mirror,” the scientist explained.

Like a giant reflector, the white ice sends much of the Sun’s energy back into space. But as it melts, the darker ocean beneath absorbs that heat instead, warming the water and accelerating the loss of ice.

The consequences are far reaching. Ocean currents carry heat far beyond the North Pole, influencing marine ecosystems and climate patterns across the planet.

As Arctic ice disappears, these circulation systems could be disrupted, with consequences scientists are still struggling to predict.

“We have models, but we don't know when, how, and what will be the exact impacts,” Mr. Geoffroy acknowledged.

The central Arctic remains poorly studied. Firsthand observations are crucial to improving climate models and predicting what lies ahead.

From ancient life to an uncertain future

But the team's questions go far beyond climate forecasts, reaching into one of humanity's oldest mysteries: the origins of life.

Could life on Earth have begun in sea ice?

Mr. Geoffroy pointed to organisms that survive extreme cold thanks to antifreeze proteins, and to the intriguing hypothesis that frozen environments may have played a role in life's earliest beginnings.

Other researchers on board are tackling a more practical mystery: how many fish live in the central Arctic Ocean?

Despite growing commercial interest, researchers still don't know whether its waters could sustain fisheries without threatening fragile ecosystems.

“To understand the loss of biodiversity and protection of biodiversity, you need to know what is there,” the scientist explained.

The research programme brings together 80 scientists and some 220 research protocols to investigate everything from how marine life responds to warming to the ocean’s role in storing carbon.

The Secretary-General, a longstanding advocate for ocean protection, smiled when he heard Mr. Geoffroy describe the international effort as a "miniature United Nations for Arctic science".

But while researchers race to understand the disappearing ice, others are already looking to profit from its retreat.

© Sébastien Devrient

New shipping routes, new battles

On their way north, the scientists encountered another unmistakable sign of change: oil tankers navigating the Northeast Passage along Russia’s Arctic coast.

The retreating ice makes the route more accessible but increases the risks of pollution and accidents.

“I can guarantee you that we saw a lot of oil tankers going through that passage,” Mr. Geoffroy told the Secretary-General. “So, it's not just a forecast. It is happening.”

An oil spill in these waters could be disastrous. Petroleum can become trapped in the ice for long periods, threatening marine life and making cleanup exceptionally difficult.

Commercial interests are not the only ones turning their attention north. Guterres pointed to tensions surrounding Greenland and the growing strategic importance of the Arctic, warning that countries increasingly viewing the region through a security lens could threaten the very environment scientists are trying to understand.

For Mr. Geoffroy, whose expedition brings together researchers from 12 countries, the question was whether science could help bridge those geopolitical divides.

“I think that is a central battle we have now. The battle for truth and the battle for science,” the UN chief replied.

The Secretary-General accused powerful economic interests, particularly those linked to fossil fuels, of seeking to obscure scientific evidence and undermine its role in public debate.

“We went from the climate denial to the climate [...] delay and ‘green hushing’,” Mr. Geoffroy observed, lamenting how climate action has slipped down political agendas despite decades of scientific warnings.

© Sébastien Devrient

A sense of urgency, and fury

Before ending their conversation, the UN chief invited Mr. Geoffroy to imagine addressing world leaders gathering at COP31.

The scientist’s message was clear:

“The findings of this science [...] need to be trusted, they need to be followed and they need to be supported.”

For Guterres, the warning struck a personal chord. He recalled visits to Antarctica and the Himalayas, where he had witnessed glaciers retreating.

Those experiences, combined with the continued refusal of some political leaders to act, had left him with more than concern.

“All these things I think have created in me a sense of urgency and, to be honest, also a sense of fury,” he admitted. “It’s an existential battle.”

In the Arctic, the researchers will continue their slow drift through the polar darkness, gathering evidence from a region changing before their eyes.

Örkki the dog will keep watch for polar bears while the team measures the ice, water and atmosphere. Thousands of kilometres away, world leaders will gather in Antalya, Türkiye at COP31 to negotiate how to confront the climate crisis.

And while the scientists have no control over where the ice carries them, the future they are documenting remains a matter of human choice.

Follow the latest developments from COP31 through our new podcast, Talk & Action, and our special daily coverage of the conference.

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos a la deriva en hielo ártico revelan cambios climáticos urgentes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Un equipo de 12 científicos y un perro llamado Örkki están a bordo de la estación polar Tara, un barco francés de investigación congelado intencionalmente en el hielo del Ártico. Esta expedición forma parte de un proyecto internacional de 20 años para estudiar cómo está cambiando el océano Ártico debido al rápido derretimiento del hielo.

**Qué pasó** – Desde agosto, la estación Tara ha estado a la deriva con el hielo sobre aguas profundas del Ártico, recopilando datos importantes sobre el calentamiento acelerado de la región. El equipo sigue los pasos de un explorador de 1893, pero en un Ártico muy diferente, con menos hielo y zonas abiertas de agua. Su investigación incluye estudiar el hielo marino, la vida marina y cómo el calentamiento afecta las corrientes oceánicas.

**Impacto** – El Ártico se está calentando entre tres y cuatro veces más rápido que el resto del planeta. El derretimiento del hielo reduce el “espejo” natural de la Tierra que refleja la luz del sol, haciendo que los océanos absorban más calor y acelerando el cambio climático. Estos cambios afectan el clima y los ecosistemas de todo el mundo. Sin embargo, muchos líderes políticos subestiman estos riesgos. Los hallazgos de la expedición son clave para mejorar las predicciones climáticas y proteger los ecosistemas frágiles ante el creciente interés comercial y nuevas rutas marítimas.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos continuarán recolectando datos durante la noche polar para entender mejor el futuro del Ártico. Su trabajo apoya las negociaciones climáticas globales en la próxima conferencia COP31, donde los líderes decidirán cómo enfrentar la crisis climática. La investigación también busca unir a los países a través de la ciencia, pese a las crecientes tensiones geopolíticas en la región.

**Frase clave** – Un equipo científico a la deriva en el Ártico muestra cómo el rápido derretimiento del hielo afecta a todo el planeta y pide a los líderes confiar en la ciencia para actuar contra el cambio climático.
